marble.name: Coin Values
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Recognise and know the value of different coins and notes
marble.prompt: If you is given a handful of coins, can they name each one — like 2p, 5p, 20p — and sort them from least to most valuable?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about measurement in everyday life — telling time to the hour and half-hour, comparing lengths and weights of objects, understanding money, and using time words like yesterday and tomorrow.

misconceptions: Judges value by physical size or colour (a 2p is bigger than a 5p, so 'worth more')
Thinks more coins means more money (a pile of pennies beats a single £2)
Confuses one penny and one pound
Doesn't recognise notes as money, or treats all notes as the same value
representations: Coins ordered on a value line (1p to £2)
A 'worth' label held separate from the coin's appearance
authoredAnswer: Says the 5p is worth more than the 2p BECAUSE 5 is more than 2 (its value, not its size); says the single 50p is more money than ten pennies (50 > 10) despite fewer coins; says £2 > 50p and £10 > £5 by their values.
probe: Put a heap of ten 1p coins next to a single 50p. Ask the child to PREDICT which is more money and, crucially, WHY, before anyone counts. Then count the value of the heap together (10p) against the 50p. A child who predicted the heap 'because there are more' meets the moment where fewer coins are worth more.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: On the reason tier says the 2p is worth more 'because it is bigger'
wrongAnswers.fix: Confront directly — compare the printed values; handle a small high-value coin against a big low-value one repeatedly, always asking 'what does it say it is WORTH?'.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The ten 1p coins, because there are more of them
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Picks the ten 1p coins over the 50p 'because there are more'
wrongAnswers.fix: Confront by counting the VALUE of each set (ten 1p = 10p vs 50p); show that one coin can be worth more than many.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Treats a 1p and a £1 as the same, or says £1 is 'one'
wrongAnswers.fix: Distinguish the two explicitly with real coins; say a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies rather than 'a hundred times bigger', which invites the size confusion.

before.name: Reading and writing numbers to 20
before.reason: Recognising coin values requires reading numerals (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)
